steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Causes: long-term (structural: economic, social, ideological) vs short-term (triggers, contingent events)

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Turning points: moments of decisive change; evaluate extent of change vs continuity after

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Change vs continuity: what changed, what stayed same; rate, direction, depth of change

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Structural forces: demography, economy, geography; Contingent: individual decisions, accidents, weather

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Q: To what extent was 1066 a turning point in English history? --- Solution: Significant change: Norman elite replaced Anglo-Saxon, feudalism introduced, language (French influence), church reform, castle-building, Domesday Book. Continuity: shire system, common law roots, parish structure, monarchy institution. Assessment: political/cultural rupture but administrative continuity

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Analyse causes of the French Revolution: long-term vs short-term | Was 1918 a turning point for women in Britain? | Compare change/continuity in Tudor religious policy

steps.title: Lesson plan
steps.body: Starter (5 min): Recall prior knowledge of themed study: key eras with quick questions. Teaching (15 min): Work through each of the learning objectives, explaining principles step by step. Key points review (5 min): Revisit the key points together, confirming understanding. Worked example (10 min): Model the example question: To what extent was 1066 a turning point in English history?. Solution: Significant change: Norman elite replaced Anglo-Saxon, feudalism introduced, language (French influence), church reform, castle-building, Domesday Book. Continuity: shire system, common law roots, parish structure, monarchy institution. Assessment: political/cultural rupture but administrative continuity Practice (10 min): Students attempt the practice questions independently; circulate and support
